new.title: Climb up inside the Porta Nigra
new.desc: The darkened Roman city gate from around 170 AD has several storeys, and you can wander through its upper storeys instead of just snapping it from the square.
new.tip: Go up first thing in the morning, before the tour groups arrive.

new.title: Get lost in the tunnels under the Kaiserthermen
new.desc: The Imperial Baths were never finished, but the real fun is below ground: a maze of service passages that once kept the baths running.
new.tip: On weekends there are evening guided tours; afterwards stroll through the Palastgarten next door.

new.title: Descend into the Amphitheater cellar
new.desc: Up to 20,000 spectators once watched games in this arena at the foot of the Petrisberg. The cellar beneath the arena floor is where lead curse tablets were found.
new.tip: Leave enough time for the cellar; then walk uphill to the start of the Weinkulturpfad right above the arena.

new.title: Feel tiny inside the Konstantinbasilika
new.desc: Emperor Constantine's 4th-century audience hall is one huge Roman brick room, now a Protestant church. Standing inside makes the scale of Roman power very physical.
new.tip: Step out to the Baroque Kurfürstliches Palais next door and its formal Palastgarten.

new.title: Hunt for mice in Trier Cathedral
new.desc: Germany's oldest bishop's church mixes Roman walls, Romanesque towers and Baroque chapels, and keeps the Holy Robe relic. The early Gothic Liebfrauenkirche stands right next door.
new.tip: Kids (and adults) can search the cathedral for hidden mice and other animal motifs.

new.title: Cross the Moselle on the Römerbrücke
new.desc: Traffic still crosses on the Roman stone piers of Germany's oldest bridge, nearly 1,900 years after they were set in the river.
new.tip: Walk down to the riverbank to see the old piers up close.

new.title: Visit Karl Marx's birthplace
new.desc: The Baroque townhouse on Brückenstraße where Marx was born in 1818 is a museum run by the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, and draws visitors from all over the world.
new.tip: Then walk to Simeonstiftplatz near the Porta Nigra to see the large Marx statue by Chinese sculptor Wu Weishan.

new.title: Peer at the baths under the Viehmarkt glass cube
new.desc: A glass cube on Viehmarktplatz shelters Roman bath walls and the foundations of Roman houses. Most visitors walk straight past it.
new.tip: It is one of the less crowded Roman sites, so it is a good pick on a busy summer weekend.

new.title: See the Roman gold hoard at the Landesmuseum
new.desc: The Rheinisches Landesmuseum keeps the largest Roman gold hoard ever found: 2,650 coins dug up in the city in 1993. There is also the Neumagen wine ship and a huge model of Roman Trier.
new.tip: Start at the city model to make sense of every ruin you see afterwards.

new.title: Find the Gutenberg Bible in the library treasury
new.desc: The treasury of the Wissenschaftliche Bibliothek shows only around 30 pieces, but they include Carolingian manuscripts and a Gutenberg Bible, usually with hardly anyone around.
new.tip: Pair it with the Kaiserthermen, a few minutes' walk down Weberbach.

new.title: Have a glass at the Hauptmarkt wine stand
new.desc: The Weinstand on the main square is a favourite meeting point for a glass of local wine, beside the Petrusbrunnen and the 10th-century market cross.
new.tip: Grab a spot on the terrace and watch the square go by.

new.title: Dine under the old wine press at Weinstube Kesselstatt
new.desc: Local wines from the Reichsgraf von Kesselstatt estate and seasonal German cooking make this the classic Trier Weinstube, right next to the Liebfrauenkirche.
new.tip: In summer, grab a table in the shady garden and order the seasonal regional dish of the day.

new.title: Eat Kappes Teerdisch at the Kartoffelkiste
new.desc: Kappes Teerdisch, half mashed potato and half sauerkraut, often with fried blood sausage, is Trier comfort food. The potato restaurant Kiste also serves Trierer Gefüllte, meat-filled dumplings baked in cheese sauce.
new.tip: Portions are large; share a Gefüllte if you want to try both.

new.title: Taste a Roman recipe at Zum Domstein
new.desc: On the Hauptmarkt, Zum Domstein serves regional German food and, in the evening, dishes cooked from the Roman recipes of Apicius in a separate kitchen. Its cellar sits on a Roman cellar about 1,700 years old.
new.tip: Start with the Roman aperitif of dry wine, honey and spices; Roman dishes can be pre-ordered for lunch.

new.title: Drink Viez from a Porz in a corner pub
new.desc: Viez, the tart local apple wine, is UNESCO-listed intangible heritage and traditionally comes in a white stoneware mug called a Porz. Aom Ecken in Trier-Nord is a family-run cult pub that pours a good one.
new.tip: It is a weekday place and gets packed in the evening, so book or come early.

new.title: Sit by the river in old Zurlauben
new.desc: This former fishermen's village on the Moselle is lined with 18th-century houses that now hold beer gardens and wine taverns, a local favourite on summer evenings.
new.tip: Gasthaus Mosellied at number 86 is known for its fish salad.

new.title: Pair Moselle wine with hearty food at Das Weinhaus
new.desc: A wine bar with a long list of local bottles, a terrace and solid German cooking, just a few doors from the Karl Marx House.
new.tip: Wikivoyage names it among the places to try Trier classics like Himmel und Ärd.

new.title: Order an Eifel beer in the old officers' casino
new.desc: The Bitburger Wirtshaus on the Kornmarkt fills a 19th-century officers' casino with traditional food and draught beer from the brewery up the road in Bitburg.
new.tip: Sit near the Georgsbrunnen fountain outside when the weather allows.

new.title: Walk the Weinkulturpfad into Olewig
new.desc: A short trail laid out by the Olewig winegrowers climbs through vineyards above the Amphitheater, explaining slate, grapes and harvest, with views over the Olewig valley and the city.
new.tip: End with a tasting in one of the wine taverns down in Olewig, Trier's own wine village.

new.title: Hike up to the Mariensäule for the classic view
new.desc: The Madonna column on the Markusberg, across the river, gives what many call the best view of the Römerbrücke and the old town.
new.tip: Cross the Römerbrücke and follow the paths uphill; it is best in late afternoon light.

new.title: Catch the city view from the Petrisberg
new.desc: The hill above the Amphitheater, once a Roman army camp, has a viewing platform over the rooftops and the vineyards of the south.
new.tip: Combine it with the Petrispark, the former garden show grounds with lookouts and a big playground.

new.title: Take a boat from Zurlauben down the Moselle
new.desc: Passenger boats leave the Zurlauben quay for one or two hour loops or full-day trips downstream to Bernkastel-Kues, passing vineyard slopes all the way.
new.tip: Go one way by boat and come back by bus or train to see more of the valley.

new.title: Warm up at the Christmas market on the Hauptmarkt
new.desc: In Advent the main square and the cathedral square fill with wooden stalls, lights and mulled wine, framed by half-timbered houses and the cathedral towers.
new.tip: Come on a weekday evening, when it is mostly locals meeting after work.

new.title: Catch a show at the Tufa
new.desc: The Tufa cultural centre runs theatre, readings, cabaret and concerts and is a hub of the local cultural scene.
new.tip: Check the programme a week ahead; smaller shows sell out.

new.title: Unwind in Nells Park
new.desc: A quiet park in the north of the city with a pond and a rose garden, popular with locals and easy to miss as a visitor.
new.tip: Visit in June when the roses are at their best.

new.title: Look down on the Saarschleife from the Cloef
new.desc: From a quartzite ledge 180 metres above the river near Orscholz, the Saar bends into a perfect hairpin around a wooded ridge: the postcard image of the Saarland.
new.tip: Go at dawn or dusk when mist sits in the loop; the short path starts at the Cloef-Atrium.

new.title: Explore Villeroy & Boch in the old abbey at Mettlach
new.desc: The ceramics maker is based in a former Benedictine abbey on the Saar, and its Erlebniswelt tells the story of the company, founded in 1748, and three centuries of table culture.
new.tip: Have coffee in the old 'Milchladen' café and walk through the abbey park afterwards.

new.title: See the gladiator mosaic at Nennig
new.desc: In Perl-Nennig a 3rd-century floor of over three million stones shows gladiators, musicians and animal hunts. It is one of the finest Roman mosaics north of the Alps.
new.tip: Open from February to November; combine with Villa Borg a few kilometres away.

new.title: Watch the waterfall in the middle of Saarburg
new.desc: The Leukbach plunges about 20 metres right through the old town of Saarburg, between the upper and lower streets, past old mills and cafés.
new.tip: Climb on to the castle ruin above town for the view over the Saar.

new.title: Visit the old bell foundry in Saarburg
new.desc: The Mabilon family cast church bells by the Saar from 1770 until 2002. Their workshop is now a museum where the moulds and furnaces are still in place.
new.tip: It is closed on Saturdays; it is just a few steps from the waterfall.

new.title: Read the stone comic strip on the Igel Column
new.desc: In the village of Igel, a 23-metre Roman tomb pillar still stands in the open, one of the few Roman grave monuments north of the Alps that survived above ground.
new.tip: It sits right by the main road through the village, so it is an easy stop on the way to Konz or Luxembourg.

new.title: Squeeze past the Spitzhäuschen in Bernkastel
new.desc: Bernkastel's market square is ringed by gabled half-timbered houses, and just off it the tiny 1416 Spitzhäuschen leans out wider at the top than at the bottom.
new.tip: Then walk or take the shuttle up to the Burg Landshut ruin for the view over the Moselle loop.

new.title: Meet 2,000 Buddhas in a Traben-Trarbach winery
new.desc: Bruno Möhring's Art Nouveau Julius Kayser winery now holds a huge collection of Buddha figures from across Asia, with a roof garden above the Moselle.
new.tip: Walk across the bridge to Möhring's Brückentor on the Trarbach side to see more of the town's Jugendstil.

new.title: Stand in the Roman wine press of Piesport
new.desc: At the western edge of Piesport, the largest wine village on the Moselle, lie the foundations of a 4th-century Roman winery that may have pressed 60,000 litres a year.
new.tip: Look up at the Goldtröpfchen, the amphitheatre-shaped vineyard above the village.

new.title: Visit the church built into the rock at Idar-Oberstein
new.desc: The Felsenkirche from 1482 is wedged into a niche in a vertical cliff above Oberstein and reached through a tunnel cut into the mountain.
new.tip: Visits are by guided tour only, bookable through EdelSteinLand; climb the steps for the view over town either way.

new.title: Tour the Bitburger brewery and sip a fresh Pils
new.desc: Bitburg's big brewery explains its beer, history and brewing in a one-hour tour that ends in the Bit-Lounge with drinks and a pretzel.
new.tip: Register in advance, and ask early if you want an English tour.

new.title: Drink a Riesling from the Doctor vineyard
new.desc: The Bernkasteler Doctor, the steep slope above the old town, is one of the most famous Riesling sites in the world. The Doctor Weinstube in the old town is the place to try it.
new.tip: Find the Doctor fountain on the Gestade, which tells the legend of the wine's healing powers.

new.title: Taste your way through the Mosel-Vinothek in Kues
new.desc: Next to the Cusanusstift, the medieval hospital founded by Nikolaus von Kues, the Mosel wine museum and vinothek let you taste Moselle Rieslings from many estates.
new.tip: Peek into the Gothic chapel of the Cusanusstift next door.

new.title: Taste Saar Riesling in Wiltingen
new.desc: The steep slate slopes between Serrig and Konz give racy, mineral Saar Rieslings, and villages such as Wiltingen, Ayl, Ockfen and Kanzem are full of family estates with tastings.
new.tip: Walk up the Galgenberg in Wiltingen for sunset; the Saar-Riesling-Sommer festival is on the third weekend of August.

new.title: Eat Spießbraten in Idar-Oberstein
new.desc: Idar-Oberstein's signature dish is Spießbraten, a big grilled roast, alongside local specialities like gefillte Klees and Dibbelaabes.
new.tip: Das Spießbratenhaus at the Alte Kanzlei near the Mineralienmuseum is devoted to it.

new.title: Sip mulled wine in Traben-Trarbach's underground cellars
new.desc: Traben-Trarbach sits on kilometres of old wine cellars, and in Advent its Mosel Wine and Christmas Market moves into these vaults.
new.tip: Outside market season, the tourist office runs cellar tours on the last Friday of the month.

new.title: Taste Auxerrois in Perl on the Upper Moselle
new.desc: In the corner where Germany, Luxembourg and France meet, the winemakers of Perl compete for the best Auxerrois, a soft white grape rarely found elsewhere in Germany.
new.tip: Combine a tasting with the Roman villas of Nennig and Borg nearby.

new.title: Walk the treetop path above the Saarschleife
new.desc: From the Cloef-Atrium in Orscholz a 1,250-metre walkway climbs up to 23 metres through the treetops to a 42-metre tower looking straight down on the Saar loop.
new.tip: The path is step-free, so it works with a pushchair or wheelchair too.

new.title: Hike the Cloef-Pfad Traumschleife to Burg Montclair
new.desc: This premium loop of about 8 km drops through steep forest from the Cloef towards the river, around the Saar loop, whose ridge carries the 12th-century Montclair castle ruin.
new.tip: Wear proper shoes: almost half the route is narrow path, and the steep slope is demanding.

new.title: Step into a rebuilt Roman villa at Borg
new.desc: Near Perl, Villa Borg has been rebuilt on its original walls: a manor house, working baths with marble pool, a Roman kitchen and gardens full of herbs and roses.
new.tip: Look out for Roman days with legionaries and gladiators, or walk the 6 km Villa Borg Traumschleife around the site.

new.title: Squeeze through the Teufelsschlucht near Irrel
new.desc: In the sandstone of the Südeifel, the Devil's Gorge is 28 metres deep and in places only a metre wide. The Teuflische Acht loop continues past old millstone quarries to the Irreler Wasserfälle, the rapids of the Prüm.
new.tip: Start at the Naturparkzentrum Teufelsschlucht and follow the yellow figure-eight with devil's horns.

new.title: Dig for agates at the Steinkaulenberg gem mine
new.desc: Near Idar-Oberstein, Europe's only gem mine open to visitors shows amethyst and agate still in the rock along a 400-metre tunnel. Outside, you can dig for your own stones.
new.tip: Bring old clothes for the digging field; whatever you find, you keep.

new.title: Hike between the two castles of Manderscheid
new.desc: The 6 km Burgenstieg loop follows the Lieser valley to the Belverde lookout, where the Oberburg and Niederburg face each other across the river, once the border between Luxembourg and Trier.
new.tip: Start at the Kurhaus car park and go clockwise.

new.title: Circle the Meerfelder Maar crater
new.desc: This volcanic crater near Manderscheid is about 1.5 km across, one of the biggest in the Eifel, with a small lake and the village of Meerfeld tucked inside.
new.tip: Detour to the Landesblick tower; in summer, cool off in Meerfeld's natural pool.

new.title: Climb the Windklang on the Erbeskopf
new.desc: At 816 metres the Erbeskopf in the Hunsrück is the highest point in Rhineland-Palatinate. The walk-on Windklang sculpture and a wooden tower look out over the Hunsrück-Hochwald forests.
new.tip: In winter there are ski lifts here; in summer there is a toboggan run.
